To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The HIV-1 specific immune response fails in the majority of people, and in the few people in whom the immune response succeeds, the response is characterized by a high level of polyfunctionality and polyreactivity, a high level of CD4+ T cell help, a high level and diversity of epitope-specific responses, and an early onset of the response.

the cellular immune response to the HIV-1 envelope protein is the most important determinant of HIV-1 control and the HIV-specific T cells that are generated during acute HIV-1 infection are the best candidates for HIV-1 control.

the HIV-specific CD8+ T cell response in the blood and the gut mucosa are qualitatively and quantitatively different and that the HIV-specific T cell response in mucosal tissues is critical to controlling the virus.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the mechanisms that lead to the generation of HIV-1-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses, (2) the mechanisms that determine the quality of these CTL responses, and (3) the mechanisms that control HIV-1 replication and disease progression in HIV-1-infected individuals.

the mechanisms by which the cellular immune response to viruses and other pathogens can be enhanced to improve host resistance and to prevent or treat chronic viral infections such as HIV-1 and hepatitis C. HIV-1 is the most successful human pathogen ever described.
the mechanisms of immune control of HIV- 1 infection, the nature of the HIV-1-specific cellular immune response, and the role of the cellular immune system in HIV-1 pathogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the success of HIV-specific cellular immune responses in some people is not well understood and that the failure of these responses in most people is due to a combination of factors, including a lack of appropriate T-cell help, a limited repertoire of HIV-specific T cells, and the ability of HIV-1 to escape from the cellular immune response.

the HIV-1-specific cellular immune responses in the small subset of individuals who control the infection are qualitatively and quantitatively superior to those in the large majority of people who fail to control HIV-1.
HIV-specific T cells are not capable of controlling HIV-1 in the absence of antiretroviral therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cellular immune response to the HIV-1 envelope is complex, with a large number of epitopes recognized by a large number of T cells.
the cellular immune response to the HIV-1 virus has not succeeded in most people because the virus is too good.

we have a very good understanding of what the cellular immune response to an HIV-1 vaccine must accomplish and that we have a detailed understanding of the reasons that the cellular immune response fails to accomplish these goals in most people infected with HIV-1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the success of the cellular immune system in controlling viral infection is not a simple matter of the number of HIV-specific T cells.
the success and failure in the HIV-specific cellular response are determined by the interplay of the virus, the host and the immune system.
the HIV-specific T cell responses that control HIV-1 infection in some people are likely to be qualitatively different from those that fail to control the virus in most people.
